These “Blackbox models” allow us to potentially predict the performance of full devices with data that might contain many physical processes that could be too complex to predict accurately with an analytical model. Hence, we Page 39 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology consider using the measurement of TRPL, spectrally-resolved photoluminescence (SRPL) as well as spectrally-resolved light transmission curves of completed solar cells as our input from which to predict the expected JV curves using a machine-learning model. Steps in developing our machine-learning (ML) prediction model are outlined in Fig. 7.2 below. Figure 7.2. Machine-learning induced prediction model development steps. With assistance of Optigon, Inc measurement system (as introduced in Project 1), we could rapidly (within 3 seconds per sample) obtain the three physical measurements of our solar cell structures (TRPL, SRPL, spectrally-resolved light transmission). The sample collection process in Fig. 7.3 shows the multi-sample acquisition capacity of the Optigon sysytem (Milestone 1.1.1). Figure 7.3. Percent Transmission, SRPL and TRPL Data collection set-up by Optigon, Inc. Five samples are collected as a batch located on a moving trail with a total collection time less than 20 seconds in total. To start with the ML prediction model development, two important assumptions must be declared. The first assumption is that sister cells in a batch that will be used to train the ML model are consistent (of the same or similar structure) so that the measured JV curves from this batch of devices serves as an accurate ground truth for the next structure whose performance we intend to Page 40 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology predict. The second assumption is that a diode circuit equivalent model of a solar cell is a suitable model to describe the JV characteristics of the perovskite solar cells we are making. To focus on the most relevant parts of the collected data, each of the TRPL, SRPL, and Transmission data are first reduced in size, so that after processing each consists of 250 data points. We next train the ML algorithm to corelate that reduced data set to the open-circuit voltage, Voc, the short-circuit current, Jsc, and the fill factor, FF, for those same devices. From the data set of 220 devices, we randomly split the data into 212 devices that are used to train the ML code and 8 devices whose Jsc, Voc, and FF we try to predict from their Transmission, SRPL and TRPL measurements. Then we compare the predictions to the actual measurements to find the accuracy of our predictions (Fig. 7.4). Our ML code performs very well: 30% of the predicted results have a 10% discrepancy from the actual measurements, while 65% of the predicted values have less than 5% discrepancy.
